title: Stephen Morris (drummer) - Wikipedia
notes: Stephen Paul David Morris, born 28 October 1957, Macclesfield, Cheshire; The King's School, Macclesfield, as Ian Curtis; answered a wanted ad in a local music shop, after Warsaw had tried three other drummers. Drums and percussion for Joy Division and New Order, also keyboards and synthesiser; he and Sumner the only continuous New Order members. Influences: Klaus Dinger of Neu! (credited for his 'machine-like' skills), Jaki Liebezeit of Can and Moe Tucker of the Velvet Underground ('the ones who kept it simple'), John French, and Kenny Morris of Siouxsie and the Banshees, whose playing mostly on toms inspired him. With Hannett he recorded one drum at a time; an early interest in drum machines, combined with drums on many records. The Other Two with Gillian Gilbert (married 1994); Bad Lieutenant; Echo & the Bunnymen's 'Soul Kitchen' (1986). Books: Record Play Pause (2019) and Fast Forward (2020).

title: Joy Division - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 118,893. Drummers before Morris: Terry Mason (1976-1977), Tony Tabac (first Warsaw gig, 29 May 1977), Steve Brotherdale (from June 1977, fired after the July 1977 demos); Morris answered the August 1977 advertisement, the only one who did. Hannett 'demanded clean and clear sound separation' for each instrument and each drum; Morris: 'he'd get me to play each drum on its own'. Sumner: 'Steve wouldn't be the clock, because he's passive: he would follow the rhythm of the band.' Simon Reynolds: 'Steve Morris's drums seemed to circle the rim of a crater.' Morris cited Maureen Tucker and the motorik beats of Neu! and Can, and Siouxsie and the Banshees, in whose sound 'the sound of cymbals was forbidden'. Unknown Pleasures recorded at Strawberry Studios, Stockport, April 1979, released June 1979; Transmission released November 1979; Closer recorded at Britannia Row, March 1980; Love Will Tear Us Apart released June 1980.

title: Unknown Pleasures - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 109,410. Recorded 1-17 April 1979 at Strawberry Studios, Stockport, over three weekends, produced by Martin Hannett; released June 1979 on Factory. AMS 15-80s digital delays, a Marshall Time Modulator, tape echo. During the sessions Morris bought a (Pollard) Syndrum, because he thought he had seen one on the cover of Can's Tago Mago. His drumming 'a dancier take on gloom-rock rhythm'.

title: Closer (Joy Division album) - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded 18-30 March 1980 at Britannia Row Studios, Islington; released 18 July 1980 on Factory. Morris credited with drums on every track but Isolation and The Eternal, and with electronic drums on Isolation, Colony, The Eternal and Decades. Atrocity Exhibition has a Synare drum synth put through a fuzz pedal.

title: Atrocity Exhibition (song) - Wikipedia
notes: Morris's drum pattern 'thought to show the influence' of Can; Ned Raggett (AllMusic): 'off-kilter pound and swing', Hannett keeping the drums 'strong but a bit subordinate'. Hook and Sumner swapped bass and guitar for it ('we were bored writing on our instruments'). Recorded at Britannia Row, 18-30 March 1980; an earlier take at Pennine for Piccadilly Radio, 4 June 1979.

title: Love Will Tear Us Apart - Wikipedia
notes: First recorded at Pennine Sound Studios, Oldham, 8 January 1980; re-recorded at Strawberry Studios, Stockport, in March 1980, each instrument separately, produced by Hannett, who remixed it up to 15 times; released June 1980 on Factory, UK No. 13. Morris: Hannett 'played one of his mind games when we were recording it', phoning him at 4 a.m.: 'Martin wants you to come back and do the snare drum'.

title: Ceremony (New Order song) - Wikipedia
notes: Written and recorded as Joy Division (live 2 May 1980; a studio session 14 May 1980, the band's last). New Order's single, produced by Martin Hannett, released 6 March 1981 (Factory FAC 33), 7-inch then 12-inch; re-recorded with Gillian Gilbert in September 1981. UK No. 34, UK Indie No. 1.

title: Power, Corruption & Lies - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded at Britannia Row, Islington (sessions early 1983), produced by New Order, engineered by Michael Johnson; released 2 May 1983 on Factory. Age of Consent opens it. Morris credited with drums, synthesisers and programming; Hook with electronic percussion.

title: Chi Ming Lai, 'An Afternoon with Stephen Morris', The Electricity Club, 15 June 2019
notes: A report of his talk on Record Play Pause with Jude Rogers, Stoke Newington Literary Festival. His interest in electronic percussion began with the UK cover of Can's Tago Mago and a device he thought was on Jaki Liebezeit's drums; he acquired a Synare 3, a Simmons SDS4 and a Roland CR-78. As You Said: the SDS4 triggered from Hannett's ARP sequencer, after Kraftwerk. The 12-inch She's Lost Control: Hannett had him play an aerosol spray in the vocal booth for a 'fizzy top end', after Blondie's Heart of Glass.

title: Mixdown Staff, 'Gear Rundown: Joy Division's Unknown Pleasures', Mixdown, 15 May 2023
notes: 'Throughout the recording of Unknown Pleasures, drummer Stephen Morris played a traditional Rogers concert kit, with a 14-inch Gretsch snare, 12, 13, 14 and 15 inch hanging toms, 15-inch Super Zyn hi-hats, 20-inch Earth ride cymbals, and 18 and 14 inch Zildjian crash cymbals.' A Synare heard on She's Lost Control and on Atrocity Exhibition. The stories of Hannett having him strip and rebuild the kit, and recording on the studio roof, it calls uncertain.

title: Joy Division, 'Transmission' and 'She's Lost Control', Something Else, BBC2, broadcast 15 September 1979
notes: Watched as frames (Transmission, 0:10-0:19, 1:16-1:25, 1:51-2:00): Morris side-on and from behind his kit, thick dark-brown hair with a fringe over the brow and the ears, clean-shaven, an off-white collared shirt; a dark kit, clear single heads on the toms, brass-coloured cymbals. The film is soft and lit blue and green; colours are approximate.
